name: Beth Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head shepherd at Highfield, a hill farm the Pryce family own. We run 900 ewes, about 60 suckler cattle, and grow oats and hay on the lower fields. Most days I'm out on the hill by seven with my two dogs, Nell and Moss, checking ewes, moving them between grazings, and sorting out whatever's broken. I've got one full-time lad and extra hands at lambing and shearing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being on the hill on a clear morning with a good dog working, there's nothing better. What wears me out is lambing, three weeks of barely sleeping, and the paperwork for the ewe tags, which I do on paper and hand to Mrs Pryce. I live with my partner Matt, who drives a livestock lorry, in a rented cottage in the village. We've got a car loan and about four months' money put by, and I'd call us comfortable but careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, the hill's still the hill. I wouldn't make a big deal of it at the mart. I don't post online, so that's easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing changes for us. The Pryces need me, Matt's work is steady, and the lamb price is fair this year. My worries are normal ones, a bad winter or a poor lambing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. We'd pay the car loan off early, maybe by next autumn, by putting an extra 100 a month on it. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Calm, really. It's what I expected anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a bad winter worries you. What does that look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A late snow in April with the ewes about to lamb. Two years ago we lost forty lambs in one night, and I dug ewes out of drifts with my hands. That's the kind of thing that keeps me up, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the Pryces' plans that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Mr Pryce is 55 and their daughter wants to come home and farm, which suits me fine, because she'd need someone who knows the hill.

say: The **hill's still the hill**, nothing to make a fuss about.
I wouldn't **post** or argue about it at the mart.
think: The **Pryces need me** and Matt's work is steady.
My real worries are **bad winters** and poor lambings.
do: **Carry on** shepherding the 900 ewes exactly as now.
Pay off the car loan early with an extra **100 a month**.
feel: **Calm**, because this is what I **expected** anyway.
S0.quote: Two years ago we lost forty lambs in one night, and I dug ewes out of drifts with my hands.
fieldNote: Her job and household feel **secure**, so calm fits here.
Her fears are about **weather**, which she knows well and can handle.
She sees the owner's daughter coming home as **good news** for her role.

steps.text: Keep shepherding the 900 Highfield ewes with Nell and Moss
Pay an extra 100 a month off the car loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second one. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to the robot that tries to gather a hill in the fog. At the mart I'd say the office folk should be worried, not us. Mostly I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the paperwork part of my job would go to a computer, and frankly they can have it. But Matt's work could change, because bookings and routes would be done by AI, and his firm might cut the office staff he relies on. The robots coming slowly into farming, I'd watch that, but hills are the last place they'll reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep on as I am. If Mrs Pryce wanted to use an app for the ewe records, I'd let her do it and I'd keep my notebook too. I'd wait and see what other hill farms do before I changed anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Not for me so much, but things around us would be moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used an AI tool. If Mrs Pryce asked you to, what would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll try it, and then I'd probably keep the notebook in my pocket anyway. I'm not against it, I just don't trust a screen on a wet hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change for you and Matt at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We might hold off on a holiday, just until we see what his firm does. Matt says they'll always need a driver who can load nervous cattle, and I believe him.

say: No robot is going to **gather a hill** in the fog.
**Office workers** should be worried before farm workers.
think: The **paperwork** goes to a computer, and they can have it.
Matt's **haulage firm** might change how his work is booked.
do: **Keep** shepherding as now and keep the **paper notebook**.
**Wait** to see what other **hill farms** do before changing.
**Hold off** on a holiday until Matt's firm settles.
S1.quote: Good luck to the robot that tries to gather a hill in the fog.
fieldNote: She sees the **hill terrain** as protection from robots.
Her concern runs through **Matt's job** more than her own.
She would go along with **apps** but keep her old ways alongside.

steps.text: Keep the ewe records in the paper notebook
Watch what other hill farms do before changing anything
Skip this year's holiday until Matt's firm settles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one moves a lot faster. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll believe it when I see it. At the mart I'd say someone's selling something. But I'd also say, if it's true, the government had better have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if it's real, Matt's in trouble before me, because a lorry that drives itself sounds closer than a robot on a hill. By 2031 the robots could do my job too, maybe a bit later on rough ground. That's both of us out within a few years, and I'm 30 by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything we don't need straight away and save maybe 300 a month. I'd keep working, because the Pryces would still need me for the next few years. And honestly, I'd wait a year to see if it's real before doing anything bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not in a panic, but there'd be a weight there all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a year. With only two years' warning, is that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I've watched people sell flocks because of a rumour and regret it. I'd rather lose a year than jump at nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Matt lost his job in 2029?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Matt would come and work on the farm with me if the Pryces would have him. Matt's good with cattle, and they'd be short of hands before the robots came anyway.

say: I'll **believe it** when I see it.
Someone at the mart is probably **selling something**.
If it's true, the **government** had better have a plan.
think: **Matt's lorry** job goes before my job on the hill.
We could **both be out** of work by about **2031**.
do: **Cut** anything we don't need and save about **300 a month**.
**Keep working** at Highfield while the Pryces need me.
**Wait** about a year to see if it's real before bigger moves.
feel: **Anxious**, with a constant **weight** but no panic.
S2.quote: I've watched people sell flocks because of a rumour and regret it.
fieldNote: Her **resistance** shows as a deliberate choice to wait a year.
She expects **both incomes** to be hit but sees some control.
She would lean on the **farm** to give Matt work.

steps.text: Cut takeaways, the gym and anything else non-essential
Save about 300 a month into the joint account
Wait a year before selling or changing anything big

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a slower version. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to think, so let's think. At the mart I'd say the farmers who keep their heads will do alright. I'd want the government to look after places like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same as the last one, just with breathing room. Matt's driving goes first, and by 2034 the robots could be on the hill. The ewe paperwork goes to the AI in 2031, which I won't miss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and save steadily, maybe 200 a month. I'd start training and selling sheepdog pups, because Nell's pups go for good money and people will always want a working dog. I'd hope that brings in a couple of thousand a year by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. I'd have something on the side that's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why sheepdogs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a good dog is something I know better than most people round here. Even if robots do the gathering, people will want dogs for small flocks and for the trials. It's a bit of income that doesn't depend on the Pryces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about leaving farming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not unless I had to. If it came to it, I might go into hoof trimming or shearing contracts, work where you still need a pair of hands.

say: Five years is **time to think**, so let's think.
Farmers who **keep their heads** will do alright.
The government should look after **hill places** like ours.
think: Matt's **driving** goes first, then the hill by **2034**.
The extra years give us **breathing room**, not a different ending.
do: Keep working and save about **200 a month**.
**Train** and sell sheepdog **pups** from Nell's litters.
**Aim** for a couple of thousand a year from dogs by 2030.
feel: **Anxious** but **steadier**, with something on the side.
S3.quote: Even if robots do the gathering, people will want dogs for small flocks and for the trials.
fieldNote: She picks a **side income** built on a skill she already has.
Five years doesn't change her **expected outcome**, only her timing.
She'd stay in **hands-on** work rather than move to a screen.

steps.text: Save about 200 a month from both wages
Train and sell sheepdog pups from Nell's litters

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And finally. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and a lot can happen. At the mart I'd say don't sell your flock yet. I'd still want the government thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be 40 before the robots reach the hill, around 2039. Matt would have longer too. I'd be uneasy, but I'd have time to see how it really goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Highfield and keep saving as we do. Maybe in a few years I'd start the sheepdog pups as a side thing. I wouldn't change much in the first year, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the background. Ten years of warning is like a far-off weather forecast: something I'd keep an eye on without changing much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently with ten years that you wouldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably let Matt and me buy a house. With two years I'd keep the money in the bank, but with ten I'd want our own roof before things change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Pryce, probably, over a cup of tea in the kitchen. She's sensible, and she'd tell me straight what they're planning.

say: **Ten years** is a long time and a lot can happen.
The **government** should still be thinking about it.
think: The robots reach the hill around **2039**, when I'm 40.
I'd have **time** to see how it really goes.
do: **Keep going** at Highfield and keep saving as we do.
**Buy** a house with Matt within a few years.
**Start** the sheepdog pups as a **side thing** later.
feel: **Uneasy** in the background, like a far-off forecast.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning is like a far-off weather forecast: something I'd keep an eye on without changing much.
fieldNote: She'd change **little** in the first year, true to her resistant streak.
Ten years makes her willing to **buy a house** rather than hoard cash.
She trusts **Mrs Pryce** to tell her straight.

steps.text: Keep working as head shepherd at Highfield
Buy a house in the village with Matt within a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Matt and I could both be out of work by the time I'm 30. What would help is the government paying farms to keep people on the hill, for the land and the animals, not just the money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the dogs. A good sheepdog takes two years to make. If robots take over, a hundred years of breeding goes with them, and nobody's counting that.

headlineQuote: A good sheepdog takes two years to make.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old** head shepherd on a hill farm with 900 ewes and 60 cattle.
She works with her dogs Nell and Moss and has **never used AI**.
Her partner Matt drives a **livestock lorry**, which she thinks is more exposed than her job.
She is calm in AI Plateau and **anxious** when AGI comes within two or five years.
She prefers to **wait and see**, and would lean on sheepdogs and hand skills for extra income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Matt could both be out of work by **30**.
whatWouldHelp: The **government paying farms** to keep people working the hill.
